en: Thus have I heard— The Discourse to Saccaka the Great (Mahāsaccakasutta), Majjhima Nikāya 36.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One desired to enter Vesālī for alms.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-son, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the Great Wood, the Gabled Hall.
The Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, here comes Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta, a debater who speaks with the airs of a scholar and is esteemed as a good man by many people."
“Venerable sir, this man desires disrepute for the Buddha, disrepute for the Dhamma, and disrepute for the Saṅgha.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would sit for a moment out of compassion.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the cultivation of the body, but not to the cultivation of the mind.
For they, Master Gotama, experience bodily painful feelings.
Once in the past, Master Gotama, when one was touched by a bodily painful feeling, even a paralysis of the thighs occurred.”
"His heart will burst, warm blood will gush from his mouth, and he will fall into madness and mental derangement.
For his mind, Master Gotama, follows the lead of the body; it functions under the control of the body."
For what reason?
Because of the lack of development of the mind.
But, Master Gotama, there are some recluses and brahmins who dwell devoted to the practice of developing the mind, but not the body.
"Master Gotama, they indeed touch you with mental painful feeling.
Formerly, Master Gotama, when one was touched by mental painful feeling, there would even be a paralysis of the thighs,
the heart would burst, and warm blood would gush from the mouth."
He will even reach madness and mental derangement.
For his body, Master Gotama, follows the mind; it operates under the influence of the mind. And why is that?
“Because of the lack of development of the body.
Therefore, Master Gotama, this occurs to me:
‘Surely the disciples of Master Gotama dwell devoted to the practice of developing the mind, and not to the development of the body.’”
“But how have you heard, Aggivessana, about the development of the body? “Such as this:
Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla.”
"Master Gotama, these naked ascetics— those who go about unclothed, who wipe their hands [clean], who do not accept 'Come, sir,' nor 'Stay, sir,' nor what is brought forward,
nor what is specially prepared, nor an invitation— they do not accept from the mouth of a jar, nor from the mouth of a basket, nor across a woolen blanket,
nor across a staff, nor across a pestle, nor from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing."
They do not go among men, nor in crowds, nor where she is present, nor where flies are swarming;
they do not eat fish, nor meat, nor drink fermented liquor, spirits, or grain-beer.
They live as one-houseers or one-mealers, or as two-houseers or two-mealers... up to seven-houseers or seven-mealers.
“They subsist on one alms-meal a day; they subsist on two alms-meals a day...

up to seven alms-meals a day. They take food once every day; they take food once every two days... up to once every seven days. Thus, in this way, they dwell devoted to the practice of taking food at intervals, even for as long as half a month.
“But, Aggivessana, do they subsist by that much alone?”
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
Sometimes, Master Gotama, they eat choice solid foods, eat choice meals, drink choice drinks, and consume choice beverages.
They indeed cause this body to gain strength, to grow, and to become plump.”
“Aggivessana, as you abandon what was before and accumulate what comes after, such is the accumulation and depletion of this body.
But how, Aggivessana, have you heard of the cultivation of the mind?
When Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta was thus questioned by the Blessed One regarding the cultivation of the mind, he was unable to provide an answer.
Then the Blessed One said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta:
“Aggivessana, even that previous bodily cultivation you spoke of is not a righteous bodily cultivation according to the discipline of the Noble One.
You do not even know what bodily cultivation is, Aggivessana; how then could you know mental cultivation?”
"Moreover, Aggivessana, there is one who has neither developed the body nor developed the mind, and there is one who has both developed the body and developed the mind.
Listen to this and pay close attention; I shall speak.
"Yes, sir," Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind?
Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in an uninstructed worldling."
Thus, being touched by a pleasant feeling, he becomes lustful for that pleasure and falls into a state of lust for pleasure.
That pleasant feeling of his ceases.
With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises.
Thus, being touched by painful feeling, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.

For him, Aggivessana, even pleasant feeling that has arisen remains obsessing the mind because the body is uncultivated; even painful feeling that has arisen remains obsessing the mind because the mind is uncultivated.
For anyone, Aggivessana, in whom pleasant feeling that has arisen in this way [obsesses the mind] on both sides...
Because the body has not been developed, arisen painful feelings persist, taking hold of the mind;
because the mind has not been developed, they persist. In this way, Aggivessana, one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind?
"Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in the instructed noble disciple.
When touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not become lustful for the pleasure, nor does he fall into a state of lustful attachment to it.
That pleasant feeling of his ceases."
With the cessation of a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises.
Being touched by that painful feeling, he does not grieve, does not lament, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.

For him, Aggivessana, even when a pleasant feeling has arisen, it does not remain obsessing the mind because of the cultivation of the body; even when a painful feeling has arisen, it does not remain obsessing the mind because of the cultivation of the mind.
“Aggivessana, for anyone in whom pleasant feelings that have arisen on both sides do not persist by obsessing the mind because the body has been developed,
and unpleasant feelings that have arisen do not persist by obsessing the mind because the mind has been developed—
in this way, Aggivessana, one is both developed in body and developed in mind.”
“I have such confidence in Master Gotama.
For Master Gotama is one who has developed the body and developed the mind.
“Surely, Aggivessana, these words were spoken by you either out of malice or after having approached [me] closely.”
Moreover, Aggivessana, I shall explain this to you:
since I shaved off my hair and beard, donned saffron robes,
and went forth from the home life into homelessness, it is impossible that any arisen pleasant feeling should persist by obsessing the mind.
“Or that an arisen painful feeling will persist by taking possession of the mind—this is impossible.
“Surely no such pleasant feeling arises for Master Gotama as a pleasant feeling, once arisen, would persist by taking possession of his mind; surely no such [painful feeling arises for him]…”
“A painful feeling, having arisen in such a way, might persist by seizing hold of the mind.
“What else could it be, Aggivessana?
Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me:”
‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.
It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the spiritual life perfectly fulfilled, perfectly pure, like a polished shell.
Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.’
Then, Aggivessana, at a later time, while still young— with jet-black hair,

endowed with the beauty of youth, and in the prime of my life— I shaved off my hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, even against the wishes of my weeping parents who stood before me with tearful faces.
Having thus gone forth, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me:
“Dwell, venerable sir;
this is the Dhamma wherein a wise person, in no long time, might by his own direct knowledge realize for himself and abide in the attainment of the goal of his own teachers.
And so, Aggivessana, I soon and quickly mastered that Dhamma.

Thus, Aggivessana, with that much—merely by striking my lips and merely by prattling and chattering—I spoke words of knowledge and words of seniority, and I, as well as others, claimed: "I know, I see.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
"Āḷāra Kālāma does not proclaim that he has realized this Dhamma for himself through direct higher knowledge and dwells having attained it, based on mere faith alone."
"Surely Āḷāra Kālāma dwells knowing and seeing this Dhamma.
Then, Aggivessana, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma; having approached him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma:
"In what way, friend Kālāma, do you declare that you dwell having realized this Dhamma for yourself through direct knowledge and attained it?"
When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the sphere of nothingness.
Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me:
“Āḷāra Kālāma has faith, and I too have faith;”
It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who possesses energy; I too possess energy.
It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who possesses mindfulness; I too possess mindfulness.
It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who possesses concentration; I too possess concentration.
"It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who possesses wisdom; I too possess wisdom.
What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he has entered and dwells in, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge?
And so, Aggivessana, before long, I quickly entered and dwelt in that Dhamma, having realized it for myself through direct knowledge.
Then, Aggivessana, I went to where Āḷāra Kālāma was, and having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“Friend Kālāma, to what extent have you yourself, through direct knowledge, realized and attained this Dhamma and proclaimed it?
“To this extent, friend, have I myself, through direct knowledge, realized and attained this Dhamma and proclaimed it.”
‘Friends, it is to this extent that I too have realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, having attained it and dwell in it.
‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great fortune for us, friends,
that we see such a venerable one as a fellow-celibate.’

Thus, that Dhamma which I have realized for myself through direct higher knowledge, having attained it, and proclaim it—that same Dhamma you have realized for yourself through direct higher knowledge, having attained it, and dwell in.

That Dhamma which you have realized for yourself through direct higher knowledge, having attained it, and dwell in—I too have realized that same Dhamma for myself through direct higher knowledge, having attained it, and proclaim it.
Thus, the Dhamma that I know, you know that Dhamma; the Dhamma that you know, I know that Dhamma.
"Thus, as I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.
Come now, friend, let us both together lead this community.
In this way, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—his own pupil—on an equal footing with himself and honored me with great honor.
Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me:
"This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to awakening, nor to Nibbāna;
it leads only as far as rebirth in the base of nothingness. Thus, Aggivessana, having found that Dhamma unsatisfactory, I became disillusioned with it and departed.
Thus, Aggivessana, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached him, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta:
“Friend, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
When this was said, Aggivessana, Udaka Rāmaputta said this to me:
“Dwell, venerable sir;
this Dhamma is such that a wise person, dwelling in it, might before long, through their own direct knowledge, realize and enter upon their own teacher’s domain.
And so, Aggivessana, I soon and quickly mastered that Dhamma.
Thus, Aggivessana, with that much—merely by the striking of lips and mere prattle—I spoke words of knowledge and words of seniority, and I, as well as others, claimed: "I know, I see.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
"Rāma did not proclaim this Dhamma, saying 'Having realized it for myself through direct higher knowledge, I enter upon and abide in it,' merely on the basis of faith alone."
"Surely Rāma dwelt knowing and seeing this Dhamma.
Then, Aggivessana, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta and, having approached him, said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
"To what extent, friend, did Rāma declare: 'Having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in it'?"
When this was said, Aggivessana, Udaka Rāmaputta explained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me:
"Rāma indeed had faith, and I too have faith."
It was not only Rāma who possessed energy; I too possessed energy.
It was not only Rāma who possessed mindfulness; I too possessed mindfulness.
It was not only Rāma who possessed concentration; I too possessed concentration.
"It was not only Rāma who possessed wisdom; I too possess wisdom.
What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared he had entered and dwelt in after having personally realized it through direct knowledge?
Then, Aggivessana, before long, I quickly entered and dwelt in that Dhamma, having personally realized it through direct knowledge.
Then, Aggivessana, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
“Friend, did Rāma declare that he had attained and entered upon this Dhamma by realizing it for himself through direct knowledge to this extent?
“Friend, Rāma declared that he had attained and entered upon this Dhamma by realizing it for himself through direct knowledge to this extent.”
‘Friends, it is to this extent that I too have realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, having attained it and dwell in it.
‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great fortune for us, friend,
that we see such a venerable one as a fellow-celibate practitioner.’

Thus, that Dhamma which Rāma himself, having realized it through direct knowledge, having attained it, and having entered upon it, proclaimed— that Dhamma you yourself, having realized it through direct knowledge,
having attained it, and having entered upon it, abide in; and that Dhamma which you yourself, having realized it through direct knowledge, having attained it, and having entered upon it,
abide in— that Dhamma Rāma himself, having realized it through direct knowledge, having attained it, and having entered upon it, proclaimed.
"Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma directly knew, you know that same Dhamma; the Dhamma that you know, Rāma directly knew that same Dhamma.
Thus, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.
Come now, friend, lead this community."
Thus, Aggivessana, Udaka Rāmaputta, who was my fellow celibate practitioner, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with great honor.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:

"This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Thus, Aggivessana, not finding satisfaction in that Dhamma, I became disillusioned with it and departed.
Continuing my journey through Magadha in search of what is wholesome and seeking the supreme state of peace, I eventually arrived at Uruvelā, a village of the Senāyans.
There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a beautiful grove of trees, and a river flowing with clear water, with pleasant landing-stairs and lovely banks, surrounded by villages for alms-gathering.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:

“How delightful indeed is this stretch of land! How beautiful is this grove of trees! And how lovely is this river that flows with white sands and fine landing places! And there is a village for alms nearby.
This is truly sufficient for a clansman seeking to strive in his exertion.”
Then, Aggivessana, I sat right there, thinking,
"This is sufficient for striving.
Furthermore, Aggivessana, three similes occurred to me, spontaneous and never heard before.
"Just as if, Aggivessana, a wet, sap-filled piece of wood were placed in water,
and then a man were to come along carrying a fire-drill,
thinking: 'I shall produce fire, I shall manifest heat.'"
“What do you think, Aggivessana, would that man,
taking an upper fire-stick and rubbing it against that piece of wet, sap-filled wood placed in the water, produce fire and manifest heat?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“And why is that? “Because, Master Gotama, that log is wet and full of sap, and it has been placed in water.
Furthermore, that man would only be a partaker of fatigue and vexation.”
“In the same way, Aggivessana, whatever recluses or brahmins dwell neither physically nor mentally withdrawn from sensual pleasures,
and for whom the desire for sensual pleasures, the affection for sensual pleasures, the infatuation with sensual pleasures, the thirst for sensual pleasures,
and the fever of sensual pleasures have not been well-abandoned within themselves and have not been well-calmed— ”
Even if those venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means,
they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

And even if those venerable recluses and brahmins do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means, they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
“Aggivessana, this first simile occurred to me, never before heard and not previously thought of.
Furthermore, Aggivessana, a second simile occurred to me, never before heard and not previously thought of.
It is just as if, Aggivessana, there were a piece of wet, sap-filled wood, placed far from water upon dry land.”
Then, suppose a man were to come along carrying an upper fire-stick, thinking:
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, Aggivessana?
“Would that man, taking an upper fire-stick and rubbing it against that piece of moist, sap-filled wood placed far from water on dry land, be able to produce fire and manifest heat?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
“And for what reason?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, that green log would still be moist and full of sap, even though it were placed far away from water on dry land;
moreover, that man would only reap exhaustion and frustration.
“In the same way, Aggivessana, whatever ascetics or brahmins [act] both with body and mind...”

They dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures; yet whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, sensual fever, and sensual passion they have toward those sensual pleasures has not been well abandoned within them, nor has it been well stilled.
Even if those venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted asceticism, [they do not attain the goal].

They are indeed incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Even if those venerable recluses and brahmins do not experience self-inflicted feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter, they are still indeed incapable of knowledge,
vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This, Aggivessana, was the second simile that occurred to me—unprecedented and never heard before.
Furthermore, Aggivessana, a third simile occurred to me—unprecedented and never heard before.
Suppose, Aggivessana, there were a dry log, withered and hollow, lying far from water on dry land.
Then, suppose a man were to come along carrying an upper fire-stick, thinking:
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, Aggivessana?
“Would that man, taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing it against that dry wood from a cow-hair brushstand placed far from water on dry land, be able to produce fire and manifest heat?
“Yes, Master Gotama. “And why is that?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, that wood is dry and withered, and moreover, it has been placed on dry land far from water.
“In the same way, Aggivessana, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures both in body and mind—
whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, or sensual infatuation they may have toward those sensual pleasures...”
Thirst for sensual pleasures and the fever of sensual pleasures have been thoroughly abandoned and thoroughly stilled within him;
even if those venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means,
they are indeed capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— even if those venerable recluses and brahmins do not [experience] such self-inflicted...
They experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet they are indeed capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This, Aggivessana, was the third simile that occurred to me—striking, never heard before.
These three similes, Aggivessana, occurred to me, striking and never heard before.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
"What if I, having set my teeth against my teeth and pressed my tongue against the palate, were to constrain, suppress, and torment the mind with the mind?
And so, Aggivessana, having set my teeth against my teeth and pressed my tongue against the palate, I constrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind with the mind.

While I was pressing my teeth against my teeth, pressing my tongue against my palate, and with my mind forcefully restraining, suppressing, and tormenting the mind, Aggivessana, sweat poured from my armpits.
Just as if, Aggivessana, a strong man were to seize a weaker man by the head or by the shoulders and force him down, suppress him, and torment him.

In the same way, Aggivessana, when I pressed my teeth against my teeth, pressed my tongue against my palate, and with my mind restrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind, sweat poured from my armpits.
Yet, Aggivessana, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
nevertheless, my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so overcome by that painful striving.
"Even such painful feelings as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing my mind.
Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me:
'What if I were to meditate on the breathless meditation?'"
So, Aggivessana, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through both my mouth and nose.
When the inhalation and exhalation were stopped through my mouth and nose, Aggivessana, there was an intense sound of wind escaping from my ear canals.
It was just like the intense sound of a smith’s bellows being blown.
In the same way, Aggivessana, when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth and nose, there was an intense sound of winds issuing from my ear canals.

Yet, Aggivessana, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused. And my body was rigid and unpacified because of that very painful striving, being struck by the exertion.
Even such painful feelings as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing the mind.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to practice the meditation of breathlessness?
So, Aggivessana, I suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears.
“Aggivessana, when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds churned within my head. Aggivessana,
just as if a strong man were to strike one’s head with a sharp spear, even so, Aggivessana,
when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds churned within my head.”

"Moreover, Aggivessana, my energy was aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness was established and unconfused. Yet my body was agitated and not calmed because of that painful striving, as I was struck down by the exertion.
Even such painful feelings as arose within me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing my mind.
Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I were to meditate on the breathless meditation?
Then, Aggivessana, I suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalations and exhalations were suppressed through my mouth, nose, and ears, Aggivessana, there arose an extreme pain in my head.

"Just as if, Aggivessana, a strong man were to bind a firm leather thong around one’s head as a headband, even so, Aggivessana, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed through my mouth, nose, and ears, there was an extreme pain in my head.
Yet, Aggivessana, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused. And my body was agitated and uncalmed because I was so overcome by that painful striving."
"Even such painful feelings as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by taking possession of my mind.
Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me:
'What if I were to enter upon a meditation entirely without breath?'"
So, Aggivessana, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalation and exhalation had been stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, Aggivessana, violent winds cut through my belly.
Just as, Aggivessana, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice might cut through a belly with a sharp butcher’s knife; so too, violent winds cut through my belly.
"In the same way, Aggivessana, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds cut through my belly.

Yet, Aggivessana, my energy was aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness was established and undeluded. And though my body was agitated and not calmed because of that painful striving, even such painful feelings as arose did not persist by obsessing my mind."
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to practice the breathless meditation?
And so, Aggivessana, I suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears.
"Aggivessana, when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth, nose, and ears, an intense burning arose in my body.
Aggivessana, just as if two strong men were to seize a weaker man by his arms and roast him over a pit of glowing embers, scorching him thoroughly;
even so, Aggivessana, when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth, nose, and ears, an intense burning arose in my body."

Furthermore, Aggivessana, my energy was aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness was established and unconfused. Yet my body was agitated and not calmed because of that painful striving, as I was struck down by that exertion.
Even such painful feelings as arose within me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing the mind.
Moreover, Aggivessana, when the deities saw me, they said this:
“The ascetic Gotama has passed away.
Some deities said:
“The ascetic Gotama has not passed away; rather, he is passing away.”
Some deities said this:
“The ascetic Gotama has not passed away, nor is he passing away; the ascetic Gotama is an Arahant, and such is the kind of dwelling of an Arahant.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
‘What if I were to practice the total cutting off of food?
Then, Aggivessana, deities approached me and said this:
‘Do not, dear sir, practice the total cutting off of food.’”
‘If you, dear sir, should practice for the total cessation of food, we would infuse divine nutritive essence into your pores, and by that you would be sustained.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:

‘If I were to claim to have renounced everything entirely, yet these deities were to infuse divine nutritive essence into my pores and I were to be sustained by that, it would be a falsehood on my part.’”
So, Aggivessana, I rejected those deities and said, "Enough.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
"Suppose I were to take food little by little, even just a handful at a time—whether it be bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup."
So, Aggivessana, I took food little by little, drop by drop— whether it was bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup. As I was taking food little by little,
drop by drop— whether it was bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup— Aggivessana, for me...
My body reached an extreme state of emaciation.
Just as the joints of an eighty-year-old or a black creeper, even so did my limbs become through that very lack of food.
Just as a camel’s hoof, even so did my buttocks become through that very lack of food.
Just as a string of beads, even so my spine appeared with its vertebrae protruding and receding because of that very lack of food.
Just as in an old shed the rafters are sagging and collapsing, even so my ribs were sagging and collapsing because of that very lack of food.

Just as in a deep well the reflections of the stars appear far down, deep-set and sunken, even so in the sockets of my eyes the pupils appeared far down, deep-set and sunken because of that very lack of food.
Just as a bitter gourd, cut while still raw, becomes withered and shriveled by the wind and sun, even so my scalp became withered and shriveled because of that very lack of food.
Then, Aggivessana, when I thought, “I will touch the skin of my belly,” I instead grasped my backbone;
and when I thought, “I will touch my backbone,” I instead grasped the skin of my belly. To such an extent, Aggivessana...
Due to that very meagreness of food, my skin clung to my backbone.
Indeed, Aggivessana, when I intended to defecate or urinate, I would fall right there on my face due to that very meagreness of food.
Indeed, Aggivessana, while trying to comfort this very body, I would rub my limbs with my hand. To him—
Aggivessana, when I rubbed my limbs with my hand, the hairs fell from my body, rotten at the roots, because of that very meagreness of food.
Moreover, Aggivessana, when people saw me, they said: "The ascetic Gotama is black.
Some people said: "The ascetic Gotama is not black; the ascetic Gotama is dark-brown."
Some people said this: “The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown; the ascetic Gotama has a golden-hued skin.
To that extent, Aggivessana, my complexion became so pure and bright that it was actually impaired by that very lack of food.
Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me:
‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations produced by self-mortification, this was the utmost; there was nothing beyond this.

Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations produced by self-mortification, this will be the utmost; there will be nothing beyond this.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations produced by self-mortification, this is the utmost; there is nothing beyond this.’
"Yet, by means of this bitter practice of self-mortification, I do not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Could there be another path to enlightenment?
Such was my thought, Aggivessana.
“I recall, however, that while sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree in my father Sakka’s workplace,

secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”
"Could this indeed be the path to enlightenment?
Aggivessana, as I reflected, my consciousness followed after that thought:
"This very path is the path to enlightenment."
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
‘Why indeed am I afraid of that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
‘I am not afraid of that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.
Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me:
‘It is not easy to attain such happiness with a body that has reached such extreme emaciation; what if I were to take substantial food, such as boiled rice and sour gruel?’”
Then, Aggivessana, I took solid food—rice and boiled grain.
At that time, Aggivessana, five monks were waiting upon me with this thought:
“Whatever Dhamma the ascetic Gotama attains, he will declare it to us.”
But when I, Aggivessana, took solid food—rice and gruel—then those five monks, having lost faith, departed, saying:
“The ascetic Gotama has become luxurious; he has abandoned his striving and turned back to luxury.
Then, Aggivessana, having taken solid food and regained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures...
“Secluded from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is born of seclusion and filled with rapture and pleasure.
Yet, Aggivessana, even such a pleasant feeling that arose in me did not persist by obsessing my mind.”

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.
Even such pleasant feeling as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing my mind.
And with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; I experienced happiness with the body. (I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna.)
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, which the noble ones describe as: “Equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness.
Even such pleasant feelings that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not remain obsessing my mind.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
"Even such a pleasant feeling as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing my mind.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
I recollected my manifold past lives, that is: one birth... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, I recollected my manifold past lives."
This, Aggivessana, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night:
ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—just as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Even such pleasant feelings as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by taking possession of my mind.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understood how beings fare according to their kamma...
This, Aggivessana, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night.
Ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Even such pleasant feelings that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not persist by obsessing my mind.

When my mind was thus concentrated—purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability—I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus I directly knew, as it really is: "This is suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is:

"This is the origin of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
“I have directly known, as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; I have directly known, as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I have directly known, as it really is:
‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I have directly known, as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.’”
As I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the influx of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the influx of existence, and my mind was liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: "It is liberated.
I directly realized: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
This, Aggivessana, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night:
ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Even such pleasant feelings as arose in me, Aggivessana, did not remain obsessing my mind.
Moreover, Aggivessana, I recall teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds.
Yet each individual among them thought:
"The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma for my sake alone."
But it should not be viewed in this way, Aggivessana;
the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others solely for the purpose of making it understood.
At the conclusion of that very discourse, Aggivessana, while still within that same prior sign of concentration...
“I steady my mind right within, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it; it is with this that I dwell for as long as I wish.
“This is credible of Master Gotama, as it would be of an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
But does Master Gotama recall ever having slept during the day?”

“I recall, Aggivessana, that in the last month of summer, after my meal and having returned from my alms round, I would spread out my outer robe folded fourfold and lie down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, to sleep.
“Is it in this regard, Master Gotama, that some recluses and brahmins speak of dwelling in delusion?
“It is not by this much alone, Aggivessana, that one is either deluded or undeluded.”
"Moreover, Aggivessana, listen to how one is both deluded and undeluded;
attend closely, and I will speak.
"Yes, sir," Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Aggivessana, whoever has not abandoned those taints that are subject to defilement, conducive to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death—I call him ‘deluded.
For it is through the non-abandoning of the taints, Aggivessana, that one is deluded.”

"Aggivessana, whoever has abandoned those taints that are corrupting, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—I call him 'undeluded.
For it is through the abandoning of the taints, Aggivessana, that one becomes undeluded.

Now, Aggivessana, for the Tathāgata, those taints that are corrupting, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future."
"Just as, Aggivessana, a palmyra tree with its crown cut off is incapable of further growth,
even so, Aggivessana, those taints of the Tathāgata that lead to defilement, to renewed existence, to distress, to the ripening of suffering,
and to future birth, aging, and death— have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future."
When this was said, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son addressed the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
To such an extent, even when being repeatedly attacked and assailed with such pointed lines of speech, Master Gotama remains so composed.”
As he was practicing it, his complexion became radiant and the color of his face became serene,
just like that of an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Master Gotama, I recall having engaged Pūraṇa Kassapa in debate.
He too, having entered into debate with me, evaded point by point, diverted the conversation to external matters, and displayed anger, hatred, and resentment. Yet,
even as he was being repeatedly attacked and addressed with such pointed words,
the color of Master Gotama’s skin brightens and the expression of his face becomes serene, just as it would for an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
"I recall, Master Gotama, Makkhali Gosāla...
Ajita Kesakambala...
Pakudha Kaccāyana..."
When I engaged Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta...
and the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta in debate, they too, when engaged by me in debate,
evaded the issue with irrelevant replies, diverted the conversation to extraneous matters, and displayed anger, hatred, and resentment.
But as Master Gotama is being thus repeatedly assailed, as he is addressed with these pointed words of reproach,
his complexion only becomes clearer and the color of his face becomes serene, just like that of an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Come now, Master Gotama, we must go.
“We have many duties, Aggivessana; we have much to do.
“Then, Aggivessana, you may go at your own convenience.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
The Mahāsaccakasutta, the sixth, is finished.
